title.rendered: Energy-Efficient Roof Materials for Wichita Homes

content.rendered:
What Are Energy-Efficient Roofing Materials?

Energy-efficient roofing materials help Wichita homeowners reduce roof heat absorption, lower cooling costs, and improve year-round comfort. In Kansas, the best energy-efficient roof is not a single product. It is a complete system that combines reflective materials, proper ventilation, quality insulation, and expert installation.

If you’ve ever walked into your home during a Kansas summer and felt heat coming down from the ceiling, your roof is the reason. It absorbs hours of direct sunlight and transfers that heat into your home.

That is the real problem most homeowners are dealing with, whether they realize it or not.

An energy-efficient roof is designed to reduce that heat transfer. It reflects solar radiation, improves insulation performance, and helps maintain consistent indoor temperatures. In Wichita, where roof surface temperatures can exceed 140°F, the right energy-efficient roofing system can make a noticeable difference in both comfort and energy costs.

Here’s where most homeowners get misled.

They focus on energy-efficient roof materials as if the product alone solves the issue. It doesn’t. Without proper system design and installation, even high-end materials will underperform.

In this guide, we break it down clearly:

  • What are energy-efficient roofing materials and how they work
  • How different systems perform in Kansas weather
  • Which energy saving roofing material options make the most sense locally
  • Common installation mistakes that reduce efficiency
  • How to choose a roofing system that performs long-term

What Are Energy-Efficient Roofing Materials and How Do They Work?

Energy-efficient roofing materials are designed to reduce heat transfer into your home by reflecting sunlight, improving insulation, or both. The goal is straightforward. Keep excess heat out during the summer, retain conditioned air more effectively, and reduce the workload on your HVAC system.

In practical terms, that means a cooler home in the summer, more stable indoor temperatures year-round, and lower operating costs.

Here’s what most homeowners are not told.

Not all energy-efficient roof materials perform the same, and the product alone does not determine the result.

Two homes can install the same material and see completely different outcomes. The difference comes down to system design, ventilation, and installation quality. If those are not handled correctly, even a high-quality energy saving roofing material will fall short.

That is why understanding how energy-efficient roofing works, not just what materials are used, matters just as much as the product itself.

Why This Matters in Wichita and the Lower Midwest

Before you choose materials, you need to understand the environment they’re going into. Kansas puts constant stress on roofing systems.

You’re not just dealing with heat. You’re dealing with multiple factors that expose weak materials and poor installation.

  • Long, high-heat summers that push roof temperatures past 140°F and drive up cooling costs
  • Frequent hail storms that damage lower-quality roofing systems
  • Strong wind events that expose installation shortcuts and weak workmanship
  • Insurance claims that are common, but often mishandled by contractors who do not understand the process

Here’s the bottom line.

Energy-efficient roofing in Wichita is not just about lowering your electric bill. It is about installing a system that can handle extreme heat, withstand storms, and continue performing over time.

If your roof cannot hold up to Kansas weather, it does not matter how “energy-efficient” it was supposed to be.

The attic should be inspected with the roof whenever it is accessible. This identifies your decking material, helps identify leaks, and assesses the ventilation that your attic needs.
Schedule an inspection to learn whether your attic space is affecting your home’s energy efficiency. 

What You Need to Know Before Choosing Energy-Efficient Roofing

Thermal imaging can be misleading without context. If you look at an image of someone standing in Antarctica, their head may appear bright red, which makes it look like the head naturally loses more heat than the rest of the body. In reality, the head is often just the most exposed area.

Homes work the same way. Triple-pane windows, solar panels, and insulated siding can all improve energy performance, but heat still moves through the most vulnerable parts of the building envelope. In many homes, that weak point is the attic and roof system.

That is why energy-efficient roofing is not just about choosing a reflective shingle or a premium roof material. The roof has to work with the attic ventilation, insulation, roof color, underlayment, and installation details beneath it. If one part of that system is wrong, the entire system can underperform.

Before choosing an energy-efficient roof, homeowners should look at four factors:

Budget and Long-Term Value

 Energy-efficient roofing materials often cost more upfront, but the real question is how the roof will perform over the next 20 to 30 years. A cheaper roof that traps heat, fails early, or needs frequent repairs can cost more over time.

Ventilation and System Design

 If attic ventilation is not designed correctly, heat can stay trapped beneath the roof. That reduces comfort, increases strain on the HVAC system, and can shorten the lifespan of roofing materials.

Kansas Weather and Insurance Risk

 In Wichita, the roof also has to handle hail, wind, and storm-related insurance considerations. Impact resistance, documentation, and installation quality matter alongside energy performance.

Contractor Capability

A contractor should be able to explain how the material, ventilation, insulation, and installation details work together. If the conversation only focuses on shingles, you may not be getting a true energy-efficient roofing system.

How Energy-Efficient Roofing Materials Reduce Heat Transfer

If you want to make a smart decision, you need to understand what actually drives energy performance. This is not complicated, but it is often overlooked.

Solar Reflectance Index (SRI)

SRI measures how well a roofing material reflects sunlight.

A higher SRI means less heat is absorbed into your roof and attic. A lower SRI means more heat is trapped and transferred into your home.

Thermal Emittance

Reflecting heat is only part of the equation.

Materials also need to release the heat they absorb. Thermal emittance measures how efficiently that happens. If a roof holds heat, it continues radiating it into your home even after the sun goes down.

Insulation and R-Value

R-value measures how well your roofing system resists heat flow.

A higher R-value improves temperature control by limiting heat gain in the summer and heat loss in the winter.

Roof Color and Heat Absorption

Color still plays a role.

  • Lighter-colored roofs reflect more sunlight and reduce heat gain
  • Darker roofs absorb more heat, increasing cooling demand

But color alone will not fix an inefficient system, and we generally recommend choosing whichever color you think will look best on your home. It has to work with the right materials, ventilation, and installation to make a measurable difference.

How Energy-Efficient Roofing Systems Actually Work

This is where most homeowners and many contractors get it wrong.

Energy efficiency is not about choosing a “good” material. It is about how the entire roofing system performs together. Miss one component, and the system underperforms.

Reflective vs. Insulating Components

Roofing systems improve energy performance in two ways:

  • Reflective materials reduce how much heat your roof absorbs
  • Insulating components slow how heat transfers into your home

You need both. Reflectivity without insulation still allows heat transfer. Insulation without reflectivity still allows excessive heat buildup.

Ventilation and Airflow

This is one of the most overlooked factors and one of the most important.

Proper ventilation:

  • Allows heat to escape from the attic
  • Reduces moisture buildup
  • Extends the lifespan of roofing materials

Without it, heat becomes trapped and your energy-efficient roofing system loses effectiveness.

Underlayment and Roof Decking

These layers sit beneath the surface but play a direct role in performance.

Quality underlayment can:

  • Improve thermal regulation
  • Add moisture protection
  • Support long-term system durability

Lower-grade materials in these layers reduce overall performance, even if the roof looks fine from the outside.

Radiant Barriers

Radiant barriers are designed to reflect heat away from the attic.

When installed correctly, they can significantly reduce heat buildup, especially during peak summer conditions in Kansas.

Installation Is What Determines Performance

You can choose the best energy-efficient roof materials available and still get poor results if the system is not installed correctly.

That is the difference between a roof that looks good on day one and a roof that performs for the next 20 to 30 years.

This is where trained crews, proven systems, and accountability matter. In the end, materials support performance, but installation determines it.

Best Energy-Efficient Roofing Materials for Kansas Homes

Now let’s get into what most homeowners want to know. Which materials actually make sense, and which ones just sound good on paper.

Cool Roof Shingles

These asphalt shingles use reflective granules to reduce heat absorption.

Where they fit:

  • Homeowners who want a traditional look with improved performance
  • Projects where budget matters but efficiency is still a priority

Reality check:
They provide moderate energy savings, but results depend heavily on ventilation and installation quality.

Metal Roofing

Metal is one of the most effective energy-efficient roofing options available.

It reflects solar heat, performs well in Kansas weather, and lasts significantly longer than standard shingles. It also offers strong resistance to hail damage, which can impact insurance considerations. 

Best for:

  • Long-term homeowners
  • Those prioritizing durability, efficiency, and fewer replacements

Clay and Concrete Tiles

These materials provide natural thermal resistance and allow airflow between tiles, which helps reduce heat transfer.

Considerations:

  • Heavier system that may require structural reinforcement
  • Higher upfront investment

Slate Roofing

Slate is one of the longest-lasting roofing materials available and offers strong natural insulation.

Best for:

  • High-end homes
  • Homeowners focused on lifespan and long-term value

Synthetic Roofing Systems

Composite materials such as DaVinci products are engineered for durability and consistent performance.

Advantages:

  • Lighter than natural materials
  • Designed for impact resistance
  • More controlled and consistent installation outcomes

Green Roof Systems

These systems use vegetation layers installed over a waterproof membrane.

Important for Kansas homeowners:

  • Rare in residential applications
  • Require specialized design and ongoing maintenance
  • Not practical for most homes in this region

Choosing the Right Material

There is no single “best” energy saving roofing material.

The right choice depends on:

  • Your home’s structure
  • Your long-term plans
  • Your balance between upfront cost and lifetime value
  • How well the roofing system is designed and installed

If you are unsure what fits your home, request a consultation with Rhoden Roofing LLC. We will walk you through the options and help you choose an energy-efficient roofing system that performs in Kansas conditions, not just one that looks good on paper.

Energy-Efficient Roofing Materials Compared: Asphalt, Metal, Tile, Slate, and Synthetic

Choosing the best energy-efficient roofing material is not about picking the most expensive option. It is about finding the right balance between cost, lifespan, and energy performance.

Here is a simplified comparison to help you evaluate your options side-by-side.

Material Cost Lifespan Efficiency Best For
Asphalt (Cool Roof) $$ 20–30 years Moderate Budget-conscious homeowners
Metal Roofing $$$ 40–70 years High Long-term durability and efficiency
Synthetic Roofing $$$ 40–50 years High Low maintenance and consistency
Tile / Slate $$$$ 50+ years High Premium homes and long-term value

Which Energy-Efficient Roofing Material Is Best?

If your priority is maximum energy efficiency, metal roofing consistently delivers the strongest performance. It reflects solar heat effectively and releases absorbed heat quickly.

If your priority is lower upfront cost, cool roof asphalt shingles provide moderate efficiency, but only when paired with proper ventilation.

If your focus is long-term performance and durability, synthetic and tile roofing systems offer a strong balance of lifespan, efficiency, and structural reliability.

Which Roofing Materials Are Least energy-efficient?

Traditional dark asphalt shingles without reflective granules absorb the most heat. This increases attic temperatures and drives up cooling costs, especially during peak summer conditions in Wichita.

How to Choose the Right Energy-Efficient Roof for Your Home

The right choice comes down to your priorities.

  • Choose metal roofing for maximum energy savings and long-term durability
  • Choose cool roof shingles for lower upfront cost with moderate efficiency
  • Choose synthetic or tile roofing for a balance of performance, lifespan, and appearance

The deciding factor is not just the material. It is how the entire energy-efficient roofing system is designed and installed.

 

Are Energy-Efficient Roofing Materials Worth It? Cost vs Long-Term Savings

Upfront Cost

energy-efficient roofing systems cost more upfront. That is expected.

What matters is what you are paying over the life of the roof.

Energy Savings

A properly installed energy-efficient roofing system reduces heat gain during Kansas summers. The real question is how much.

In most homes, you can expect:

  • 10% to 25% reduction in cooling costs with reflective materials
  • Up to 30% less attic heat buildup with proper ventilation
  • Roof surface temperatures reduced by up to 50°F under peak sun exposure

In practical terms, that means:

  • Lower cooling costs
  • Less strain on your HVAC system
  • More consistent indoor temperatures during peak heat

For many homeowners in Wichita, this can translate into hundreds of dollars in annual energy savings, depending on home size and system design.

Long-Term Value

You are not buying instant returns. You are investing in performance over time.

That shows up as:

  • Lower energy bills
  • Fewer repairs
  • Longer roof lifespan

What Determines Your Actual Savings

Not every home sees the same results.

Your energy savings depend on:

  • Attic ventilation design
  • Insulation levels (R-value)
  • Roof color and reflectivity
  • Overall installation quality

That is why two homes with the same energy-efficient roof materials can produce very different results.

If you want a clear picture of what this looks like for your home, request an evaluation from Rhoden Roofing LLC.

 

Energy-Efficient Roofs That Are Installed the Right Way

A high-performing roof does not happen by accident. It comes from a clear, repeatable process.

At Rhoden Roofing LLC, every energy-efficient roofing system follows a structured approach:

  • Inspection – Identify heat loss, ventilation issues, and existing damage
  • Recommendations – Match materials and system design to your home, goals, and budget
  • Insurance Assistance (if needed) – Guide the claim process so nothing is overlooked
  • Installation – Install the complete system correctly, not just the surface materials
  • Final Walkthrough – Confirm the system is installed properly and ready to perform

No guesswork. No shortcuts. Just an energy-efficient roofing system built for long-term performance.

Energy-Efficient Roofing Questions Wichita Homeowners Ask Before Replacing Their Roof

Before you move forward with an energy-efficient roof, you need clear answers. These are the most common questions homeowners ask when they want to get it right the first time.

What are energy-efficient roofing materials?

Energy-efficient roofing materials are designed to reduce heat transfer into your home. They reflect sunlight, improve insulation, or both. The result is lower attic temperatures and reduced strain on your HVAC system over time.

Is a new roof considered an energy-efficient improvement?

Yes, when it includes modern materials and proper system design. Upgrading ventilation and using higher-performance materials can significantly improve how your home manages heat compared to an older roof.

What is the best energy-efficient roofing material for Kansas homes?

The best energy-efficient roof depends on your home and goals. Metal roofing and reflective shingles are common choices, but durability, reflectivity, and installation quality ultimately determine performance.

Do energy-efficient roofing materials lower energy bills in Wichita?

Yes. By reducing heat gain during peak summer months, energy-efficient roofing systems lower the demand on your cooling system, which reduces overall energy use.

Does roof color make a difference?

Yes. Lighter-colored roofs reflect more sunlight, while darker roofs absorb more heat, increasing cooling demand. Color plays a role, but it must work with the full roofing system to be effective.

How important is ventilation?

Ventilation is critical. It allows heat to escape the attic, preventing buildup that reduces efficiency and shortens the lifespan of your roofing system.

Are energy-efficient roofing materials worth the cost for Kansas homeowners?

Yes, when installed correctly. Lower energy bills, fewer repairs, and longer lifespan typically outweigh the higher upfront cost.

Do energy-efficient roofing materials qualify for tax credits or rebates?

Some materials may qualify if they meet ENERGY STAR or U.S. Department of Energy standards. Not all products are eligible, and local rebates may vary.

How do I know if my new roof qualifies for an energy tax credit?

Eligibility depends on meeting performance standards and having proper documentation, including manufacturer certifications and installation details. Requirements can change, so it is important to verify before starting your project.

Are tax credits enough to justify the cost of an energy-efficient roof?

Tax credits can reduce upfront cost, but the primary value comes from long-term performance. Lower energy use, reduced HVAC strain, and longer lifespan are what make the investment worthwhile.

title.rendered: Can I Replace Just One Side of My Roof?

content.rendered:
What Homeowners Need to Know About Partial Roof Replacement

After a hailstorm in Wichita, KS, one of the most common questions we hear is whether a partial roof replacement is enough.

Sometimes the insurance adjuster only approves one slope.
Sometimes only one side looks damaged from the ground.
Sometimes the homeowner is focused on lowering the partial roof replacement cost instead of replacing the whole roof.

A partial roof replacement can work in the right situation, but it often creates problems when the rest of the roof is already worn. We regularly see homeowners dealing with mismatched shingles, limited warranty coverage, and insurance disputes after choosing a partial repair instead of a full replacement. Many of those situations start with the same questions:

  • does homeowners insurance cover roof replacement
  • does insurance cover roof replacement
  • how to get insurance to pay for roof replacement
  • will insurance approve full replacement instead of partial roof replacement

At Rhoden Roofing, we deal with these decisions every week across Wichita, KS and Sedgwick County. The right answer depends on roof age, storm damage, material availability, and what the insurance policy actually allows. A proper inspection often shows that the lowest partial roof replacement cost is not always the best long-term decision.

In this guide, we’ll explain when partial replacement works, when it doesn’t, how insurance affects the decision, and why many homeowners in Wichita, KS end up replacing the entire roof even when only one side looks damaged.

We See This Situation All the Time in Wichita After Hail Storms

Most partial roof replacement projects in Wichita, KS start after a storm.

A homeowner notices damage on one side.
An insurance claim gets filed.
The adjuster approves repairs on one slope but not the whole roof.

Now the homeowner has to decide whether to accept the repair, pay the difference, or figure out how to get insurance to pay for roof replacement instead of approving only part of the job.

This is where experience matters.

Kansas weather is hard on roofing systems. Hail, wind, heat, and freezing temperatures can damage more than what you see from the yard. During inspections in Wichita, KS, we often find lifted shingles, broken seal strips, and decking damage that wasn’t included in the first insurance estimate.

We also see situations where shingles are discontinued or faded, which makes a partial roof replacement difficult even if only one side looks damaged. When that happens, homeowners start comparing the partial roof replacement cost to the cost of replacing the entire roof and asking whether insurance will cover more than the first approval.

Because Rhoden Roofing handles storm claims every week in Wichita, KS, we look at the entire system, not just the visible damage. Sometimes a partial repair works. Sometimes it leads to more repairs, more cost, and more frustration later.

The difference comes down to understanding what the roof actually needs, not just what the first estimate says.

When Partial Roof Replacement Makes Sense (and When It Doesn’t)

A partial roof replacement means replacing shingles on one section of the roof instead of installing a full system. While this is often the suggestion of insurance companies, we rarely do partial roof replacements. 

Partial replacement may work when:

  • the roof is still in good condition
  • matching shingles are available
  • the damage is isolated
  • the rest of the roof still has years of life left

Tying a new roof in with an existing roof is likely will produce inconsistencies, and those inconsistencies make it difficult for the manufacturer or installer to offer a substantive warranty.

We also see problems when homeowners focus only on partial roof replacement cost without looking at long-term performance. A lower price today doesn’t help if the rest of the roof fails in a few years.

In Wichita, KS, partial replacement works best on newer roofs with isolated damage. On older roofs, or after major hail storms, a full replacement is nearly always the smarter investment, especially when homeowners are already asking if insurance will cover roof replacement or trying to understand how to get insurance to pay for roof replacement instead of covering only one side.

Why Partial Roof Replacement Often Costs More Long-Term

One of the biggest reasons homeowners ask about partial roof replacement is cost. Replacing one slope sounds cheaper than replacing the entire roof, and at first the partial roof replacement cost usually is lower.

But the upfront price doesn’t tell the whole story.

When only part of the roof is replaced, the remaining section keeps aging. If that side fails later, the homeowner pays for tear-off, labor, and materials again. We see this often in Wichita, KS, especially after multiple storms hit the same roof over time.

Typical scenario:

  • replace one side now
  • replace the rest later
  • pay labor twice
  • deal with mismatched shingles
  • lose warranty coverage
  • file another insurance claim

Once homeowners see the real numbers, the difference between partial roof replacement cost and full replacement is usually smaller than expected. We explain this in more detail in our guide on roof replacement cost and long-term value, where we break down how homeowners in Wichita, KS should compare repair vs replacement before making a decision.

Why Partial Roof Replacement Can Affect Your Warranty

This is one of the biggest issues homeowners don’t hear about until after the work is done.

Roofing warranties are written for complete systems, not half-old and half-new roofs. When only one side is replaced, you’re combining new materials with an existing roof that may already be worn down. That can create problems with both manufacturer warranties and workmanship coverage, especially when the project started as a partial roof replacement instead of a full installation.

Manufacturer warranties usually require the roof to be installed as a complete system with approved underlayment, ventilation, flashing, and accessories. When only one slope is replaced, those conditions may not be met, which can limit what the warranty actually covers. This is one reason a lower partial roof replacement cost doesn’t always mean better value.

Workmanship warranties can also be affected. Some contractors only warranty the section they replaced, which means the homeowner is responsible if the rest of the roof fails later. We see this situation in Wichita, KS more often than people expect, especially after storm repairs where insurance only approved part of the roof.

At Rhoden Roofing, warranty protection is one of the main reasons we look carefully at whether a partial roof replacement makes sense. We offer a Lifetime Workmanship Warranty on qualifying installations, and that level of coverage only works when the entire roofing system is installed correctly. When a roof is pieced together over time, it becomes harder to stand behind the work long-term.

Many homeowners start asking does insurance cover roof replacement or does homeowners insurance cover roof replacement once they realize warranty coverage may be limited with a partial repair.

What Happens If Your Shingles Can’t Be Matched?

Matching shingles is one of the biggest reasons insurance claims turn into full replacements in Wichita, KS.

Even if the same brand is still available, the color on your roof has likely faded over time. When new shingles are installed next to older ones, the difference is often conspicuous, even from the ground. That may not affect performance, but it affects appearance, resale value, and sometimes insurance approval.

In other cases, the original shingles are discontinued. Manufacturers change product lines often, and when an exact match isn’t available, a partial roof replacement may not restore the roof to its original condition. When that happens, homeowners start asking:

  • does homeowners insurance cover roof replacement
  • does insurance cover roof replacement
  • how to get insurance to pay for roof replacement
  • will insurance approve full replacement instead of partial roof replacement

Insurance companies look at whether the roof can be repaired properly. If matching materials are not available, the partial roof replacement cost may not matter, because the repair may not meet policy requirements.

During inspections in Wichita, KS, we check the age of the shingles, the manufacturer, the color, and whether matching products are still available. If the roof cannot be repaired without creating a mismatch, a full replacement may make more sense than a partial fix.

Does Homeowners Insurance Cover Partial Roof Replacement?

After storm damage, one of the first questions homeowners ask in Wichita, KS is whether insurance will pay for the whole roof or only part of it.

Common searches include:

  • does homeowners insurance cover roof replacement
  • does insurance cover roof replacement
  • how to get insurance to pay for roof replacement

The answer depends on the policy, the damage, and what the inspection shows.

Sometimes the adjuster only approves repairs on one slope. When that happens, the homeowner has to decide whether to accept a partial roof replacement, request a review, or provide additional documentation.

Insurance companies typically look at:

  • age of the roof
  • type of damage
  • number of slopes affected
  • matching requirements
  • local building codes
  • policy coverage

In many cases, the first estimate doesn’t include everything. During inspections in Wichita, KS, we often find additional damage or matching issues that change the scope of the claim. When that happens, the approval may move from a partial repair to a full replacement.

Understanding the real partial roof replacement cost compared to full replacement is important here, because insurance coverage can make the difference smaller than expected.

How to Get Insurance to Pay for Full Roof Replacement Instead of One Side

One of the most common questions homeowners ask after a storm is how to get insurance to pay for roof replacement instead of approving only a partial roof replacement.

The answer isn’t about arguing with the insurance company. It’s about having the right inspection, the right documentation, and a contractor who understands how claims work in Wichita, KS.

Insurance companies make decisions based on what they see and what the policy allows. If the inspection only shows damage on one slope, they may approve a partial repair. But that doesn’t always mean the rest of the roof is in good condition.

A more detailed inspection can reveal problems like:

  • damage on multiple slopes
  • discontinued shingles
  • code requirements that require upgrades
  • decking damage under the shingles
  • seal strip damage from hail
  • ventilation issues affecting the whole roof

When this information is documented correctly, the claim can sometimes be reviewed again. That’s often how homeowners go from a partial roof replacement approval to a full replacement.

This is also why homeowners start comparing the partial roof replacement cost to the total replacement cost and asking whether insurance will cover more once the roof is evaluated properly.

At Rhoden Roofing, we work with homeowners and adjusters across Wichita, KS to make sure the roof is inspected correctly the first time. Not every claim becomes a full replacement, but many do once all the damage is documented.

Kansas Weather Is Hard on Roofs — Why Full Replacement Often Makes More Sense

Kansas weather is one of the biggest reasons a partial roof replacement doesn’t always hold up long-term.

In Wichita, KS, roofs deal with strong winds, large hail, extreme heat in the summer, and freezing temperatures in the winter. Those conditions wear roofing materials down faster than many homeowners expect, especially on older roofs.

When only one side of the roof is replaced, the new section may perform well, but the older section keeps aging. That can lead to leaks, lifted shingles, and more repairs sooner than expected. It also means the roof won’t wear evenly, which affects both performance and appearance.

We see this often when homeowners focus only on the partial roof replacement cost without considering how the rest of the roof will hold up after the next storm season.

A full replacement allows the roof to be installed as one complete system with proper ventilation, underlayment, flashing, and manufacturer-approved materials. That makes warranty coverage stronger and reduces the chances of needing another repair after the next hailstorm.

This is why many homeowners in Wichita, KS start by asking does insurance cover roof replacement, but after a full inspection decide that replacing the entire roof once is the better long-term investment.

When a Full Roof Replacement Is the Smarter Investment

Homeowners often focus on the price difference between a full replacement and a partial roof replacement, but the better way to look at it is long-term value.

The partial roof replacement cost may be lower today, but that doesn’t mean it’s the smarter decision. If the roof is older, has already been repaired, or has been through multiple storms, replacing only one side often leads to more work later. We see this often in Wichita, KS, where hail and wind damage can shorten the life of a roof faster than homeowners expect.

A full replacement resets the lifespan of the entire system. That means:

  • one tear-off instead of two
  • one installation instead of multiple repairs
  • full warranty coverage
  • better performance in future storms

Insurance also plays a big role in this decision. Many homeowners start by asking does homeowners insurance cover roof replacement or does insurance cover roof replacement, and the answer can change the numbers completely. When insurance pays for part of the work, the difference between the total replacement cost and the partial roof replacement cost is often smaller than expected.

If you want a full breakdown of what the replacement process involves, what materials last the longest in Kansas weather, and how to plan for the cost, we cover it step-by-step in The Complete Homeowner’s Guide to Roof Replacement in Kansas, where we explain what homeowners in Wichita, KS should know before deciding between repair, partial roof replacement, or full replacement.

A complete replacement allows the roof to be installed as one system with proper ventilation, underlayment, flashing, and manufacturer-approved materials. That’s the kind of installation that holds up better in Kansas weather and makes it possible to offer stronger warranty protection.

Why Wichita Homeowners Trust Rhoden Roofing for Roof Replacement and Insurance Claims

Choosing between a full replacement and a partial roof replacement isn’t just about price. It’s about working with a contractor who understands how roofing systems actually perform in Wichita, KS, and who will still be here years after the job is done.

Rhoden Roofing installs residential, commercial, and multi-family roofing systems designed to hold up in Kansas weather. We are certified with leading manufacturers including GAF, Malarkey, DaVinci, and Ludowici, which allows us to install complete roofing systems using approved materials and methods.

We are also a GAF President’s Club contractor, a designation held by only a small percentage of roofing companies. That certification requires ongoing training, inspections, and proven installation quality.

One of the biggest differences homeowners notice is our approach to warranty protection. We offer a Lifetime Workmanship Warranty on qualifying roofs because we install complete systems the right way. That level of coverage is difficult to offer when a roof is pieced together through a partial roof replacement, which is why we take the time to explain all options before the work starts.

We also help homeowners navigate storm damage claims. When people ask how to get insurance to pay for roof replacement, the answer usually starts with a detailed inspection and proper documentation. Because we work with insurance claims regularly in Wichita, KS, we know what adjusters look for and how to make sure the roof is evaluated correctly.

Not every claim results in full replacement, but many do once the entire system is inspected instead of only one slope.

What Most Wichita Homeowners Get Wrong About Partial Roof Replacement

The biggest mistake we see is homeowners making a quick decision after a storm without understanding how a partial roof replacement will affect the roof long-term.

Replacing one side sounds cheaper, especially when looking only at the partial roof replacement cost, but it can lead to more repairs later if the rest of the roof is already worn. In Wichita, KS, we often see homeowners approve a partial repair after the first insurance estimate, only to need another replacement a few years later.

Another common mistake is assuming every contractor gives the same advice. Some companies focus on getting the job done quickly after storms, and a partial repair is faster than evaluating the entire roof. A proper inspection takes more time, but it gives a clearer picture of what the roof actually needs.

Insurance confusion is another issue. Homeowners search does homeowners insurance cover roof replacement or does insurance cover roof replacement, but the real answer depends on the condition of the whole roof, not just one slope. In many cases, the first approval is for a partial roof replacement, but a more detailed inspection with thorough documentation can affect what insurance covers.

The goal shouldn’t be to spend the least amount today.
The goal should be to get the best value for your home’s life.

Common Questions About Partial Roof Replacement in Wichita, KS

After hail storms or insurance inspections, homeowners in Wichita, KS ask the same questions about partial roof replacement, insurance coverage, and cost.

Is partial roof replacement cheaper than full replacement?

The partial roof replacement cost is usually lower at first, but it can cost more over time if the rest of the roof needs to be replaced later. Many homeowners in Wichita, KS end up paying for labor twice when they try to fix only one side.

Does homeowners insurance cover roof replacement?

Many homeowners ask does homeowners insurance cover roof replacement or does insurance cover roof replacement after storm damage. Insurance may cover part or all of the work depending on the policy, the damage, and whether the roof can be repaired correctly with a partial replacement.

How do I get insurance to pay for full roof replacement?

When homeowners ask how to get insurance to pay for roof replacement, the answer usually comes down to inspection and documentation. If shingles can’t be matched, multiple slopes are damaged, or code upgrades are required, the claim may be approved for full replacement instead of a partial roof replacement.

Will shingles match if I only replace one side?

Not always. Sun fading, discontinued products, and storm wear make matching difficult. This is one reason many homeowners in Wichita, KS choose full replacement instead of partial repair.

Does a partial roof replacement affect the warranty?

Yes. Most warranties are written for complete roofing systems. When a roof is replaced in sections, coverage may be limited, especially if the project started as a partial roof replacement.

Not Sure If You Should Replace One Side or the Whole Roof? Start With an Inspection

If your insurance only approved one slope, don’t rush into a partial roof replacement just to get the job done. In many cases, the lowest partial roof replacement cost ends up costing more later because the rest of the roof still needs to be replaced.

The only way to know what makes sense is to inspect the entire roofing system. In Wichita, KS, roofs deal with hail, wind, and temperature swings every year, and those conditions can cause damage that isn’t visible from the ground.

At Rhoden Roofing LLC, we evaluate the whole roof, the insurance scope, and the condition of the materials before recommending a repair or replacement. If a partial roof replacement makes sense, we’ll tell you. If a full replacement will save you money long-term, we’ll explain why.

If you’re trying to figure out does insurance cover roof replacement, or wondering how to get insurance to pay for roof replacement, the first step is getting the roof inspected by a contractor who understands both roofing and insurance claims.

title.rendered: Can My Pets Handle a Roof Replacement?

content.rendered:
What Homeowners Worry About Before Roof Replacement

Before roof replacement starts, most homeowners are not worried about shingles.
They are worried about what the job will actually be like.

How long does roof replacement take?
Should I stay home during roof replacement?
Will my dog freak out?
Will my cat hide all day?
Do companies that replace roofs work on the weekends?

We hear these questions all the time from homeowners across Wichita, KS, especially after hail storms when roof replacement has to be scheduled quickly.

Roof replacement is loud, but it should not feel chaotic. When the job is planned correctly and installed by an experienced crew, most homeowners and pets handle it without any problems.

In this guide, we’ll cover:

  • How long roof replacement takes in Wichita
  • Whether you should stay home during roof replacement
  • How dogs and cats usually react to the noise
  • Whether roofing companies work on weekends
  • How to prepare your home before installation
  • What makes roof replacement go smoothly

If you want roof replacement to go as stress-free as possible, the best thing you can do is know what to expect before the work starts.

What Roof Replacement Is Really Like for Homeowners in Wichita, KS

Roof replacement is one of the loudest projects you can have done on your home, but it is also one of the fastest when the crew knows what they are doing.

During a typical roof replacement in Wichita, you will hear:

  • Footsteps on the roof all day
  • Nail guns and hammering
  • Shingles being removed
  • Dump trailers filling up
  • Trucks coming and going

This is normal.

Most roof replacement jobs in Wichita, KS move quickly because weather can change fast. Crews work efficiently to remove the old roof, inspect the decking, install underlayment, and complete the new roofing system as fast as possible without cutting corners.

Because roof replacement usually only lasts a day or two, many homeowners are surprised that the noise does not last nearly as long as they expected. That is why one of the first questions we hear is how long roof replacement takes and whether they should stay home during the work.

How Long Does Roof Replacement Take in Wichita, KS?

One of the most common questions we hear before roof replacement starts is how long does roof replacement take.

We complete most roof replacements in under one day. Larger homes, steep roofs, or repairs under the shingles can make the job take longer, but most projects are finished quickly once the crew starts.

If you are wondering how long does it take to replace a roof, the biggest factors are:

  • Size of the roof
  • Pitch and complexity
  • Weather conditions
  • Decking repairs
  • Number of layers removed
  • Material type

Storm damage can also affect how long roof replacement takes, especially if insurance inspections or supplements are needed.

We explain the full process in our complete guide to roof replacement in Kansas, including what happens before installation, during tear-off, and after the job is finished. For a behind-the-scenes look at what happens between signing your contract and the first shingle coming off, check out a walkthrough for Rhoden Roofing’s process here.

Knowing how long roof replacement takes helps homeowners plan for work schedules, pets, and whether they want to stay home during the job.

Should I Stay Home During Roof Replacement?

Many homeowners ask if they should stay home during roof replacement, and the answer is simple. You can stay home, but you do not have to.

Roof replacement is loud. There will be constant movement on the roof, hammering, and debris being removed. Some people are fine staying home, while others prefer to leave for the day, especially if they work from home or have pets that get nervous.

If you are asking should I stay home during roof replacement, think about:

  • How sensitive you are to noise
  • How long roof replacement will take
  • Whether you work from home
  • How your pets react to loud sounds
  • How comfortable you are with crews outside all day

Many homeowners in Wichita stay home the first day, then leave the second day once they realize how loud the work can be. Others plan to be gone the entire time.

Either way is fine as long as the contractor has access to the roof and driveway.

How Roof Replacement Affects Dogs, Cats, and Other Pets

Pets usually react more to roof replacement than homeowners do.

Dogs may bark at the noise.
Cats may hide.
Some animals get nervous when strangers are around the house.

This is completely normal during roof replacement, especially during tear-off.

If you have pets at home during roof replacement, a few simple steps help a lot:

  • Keep pets inside
  • Use a quiet room if possible
  • Make sure gates stay closed
  • Tell the crew you have pets
  • Consider boarding if your pet gets anxious

Most roof replacement jobs only last a short time, which is why knowing how long roof replacement takes makes planning easier for pet owners.

A good rule of thumb: if your dog barks or is stressed when it hears a knock at the door, it will bark or be stressed by a roof replacement.

Do Companies That Replace Roofs Work on the Weekends in Wichita?

Another question we hear often is do companies that replace roofs work on the weekends.

Most roof replacement projects in Wichita, KS are scheduled during the week, but weekend work sometimes happens when schedules get backed up after storms.

Roofing companies may work weekends when:

  • Storm damage creates a long wait list
  • Weather delays during the week
  • Insurance deadlines
  • Homeowner requests weekend work

Some neighborhoods or HOAs limit weekend construction, so the schedule may depend on local rules.

If timing matters, ask your contractor early how long roof replacement will take and whether weekend work is possible.

How to Prepare Your Home and Pets Before Roof Replacement

A little preparation makes roof replacement much easier.

We answer this question in-depth in another article, but some key takeaways can be found below.

  • Move vehicles out of the driveway
  • Secure pets inside the home
  • Remove fragile items from walls
  • Cover items in the attic
  • Let neighbors know work is scheduled
  • Plan where you will be during the day
  • Mow the yard
  • Move patio and breakable outdoor decor

Most roof replacement projects only last a short time, but knowing how long roof replacement takes helps you decide whether to stay home, leave for the day, or make plans for pets.

Good preparation makes the job feel much less stressful.

Why a Professional Roof Replacement Should Not Feel Stressful

Roof replacement is a big project, but it should not feel out of control.

When the job is done by an experienced crew, the process follows a clear plan:

  1. Inspection
  2. Scheduling
  3. Material delivery
  4. Tear-off
  5. Installation
  6. Cleanup
  7. Final check

At Rhoden Roofing, we install roof replacement projects across Wichita every week, and the goal is always the same — finish the job quickly, keep the site clean, and make sure the homeowner knows exactly what to expect.

When homeowners understand how long roof replacement takes and how the job will be done, the process feels much easier.

Common Questions Homeowners Ask Before Roof Replacement in Wichita, KS

Before roof replacement starts, homeowners usually want to know how long the job will take, whether they should stay home, and how the noise will affect pets. These are the most common questions we hear from homeowners in Wichita, KS when scheduling roof replacement.

How long does roof replacement take?

We complete most roof replacements in one day, from tear-off to final cleanup. Roofs larger than 50 squares, an exceptionally steep pitch, or a cut-up roof with many unique angles and corners may two days or more.

Should I stay home during roof replacement?

You can stay home during roof replacement, but many homeowners choose to leave because the noise can be constant during tear-off and installation. If you work from home or have pets that get nervous, it may be easier to be gone while the roof replacement is in progress.

Will my pets be okay during roof replacement?

Most pets are okay during roof replacement, but dogs and cats can get stressed from the noise and movement on the roof. Keeping pets inside, using a quiet room, or boarding them for the day can make roof replacement easier for both the pet and the homeowner.

Do companies that replace roofs work on the weekends?

Some companies that replace roofs do work on the weekends, but most roof replacement jobs in Wichita are scheduled during the week. Weekend work may happen after storms, during busy seasons, or when weather delays make the schedule tight.

Is roof replacement loud inside the house?

Roof replacement is loud inside the house, especially during the tear-off stage when shingles are removed. The noise usually lasts one to two days, which is why many homeowners ask how long roof replacement takes before scheduling the job.

How should I prepare my home before roof replacement starts?

You should prepare your home before roof replacement by moving cars, securing pets, protecting attic items, and knowing the schedule ahead of time. When homeowners know how long roof replacement will take, planning around the work becomes much easier.

Not Sure How Roof Replacement Will Affect Your Home? Start With an Inspection

If you are planning roof replacement and wondering how long it will take, whether your pets will be okay, or if you should stay home during the job, the best first step is a proper inspection.

Roof replacement should not feel stressful when the work is done by a contractor who installs roofs every week and understands how homes in Wichita, KS handle noise, weather, and scheduling.

At Rhoden Roofing, we walk homeowners through the entire process before the job starts so there are no surprises once the crew arrives.

If you want a roof built to last — and a company that will still be here to stand behind it — schedule your estimate with Rhoden Roofing LLC today.

title.rendered: How Much Will a Commercial Roof Coating Disrupt Tenants?

content.rendered:
Unlike full tear-offs, commercial roof coatings are designed to restore the existing roof rather than replace it. Still, understanding how the coating application process affects tenants is critical before signing a contract.

A commercial roof coating is usually less disruptive than a full roof replacement because it does not require large-scale tear-off, demolition, or removal of the existing roof system. However, “less disruptive” does not mean “invisible.”

In this article, we’ll explain what tenants are most likely to notice during a roof coating project, how long the work may take, what property owners should plan for, and how the right contractor can reduce disruption before it becomes a problem.

If you need a tenant-conscious plan tailored to your building, Rhoden Roofing LLC can help.

First: Is Your Roof Actually a Good Candidate for Coating?

Before discussing tenant disruption, it is important to clarify what this article is — and is not — assuming.

A roof coating can be a useful solution when the existing roof is still in serviceable condition. In most cases, coatings are used to extend the life of an aging but functional roof system. They are not a replacement for a roof that has already failed.

A coating may be appropriate if:

  • The roof is structurally sound
  • The existing roof system is dry
  • The membrane or metal panels are still in reasonably good condition
  • Leaks are minor, isolated, and repairable before coating
  • The roof surface can be properly cleaned, repaired, and prepared
  • Drainage conditions are acceptable for the product being used
  • The coating system is compatible with the existing roof surface

A coating is usually not the right solution if the roof has active widespread leaks, wet insulation, major drainage issues, structural concerns, serious membrane failure, failing flashings, or trapped moisture within the roof assembly.

A coating does not make a bad roof good. It adds a protective layer over the roof that already exists. If the existing roof is dry, stable, and properly prepared, that can be a useful way to defer a larger roofing project. If the existing roof is already failing, coating over it can trap problems inside the system.

For a broader explanation of when coatings make sense, start with our full guide: Flat Roof Coatings – What Are They and When Are They Appropriate?

This article assumes your roof has already been inspected, or that you are exploring a coating because it may be a legitimate fit. From there, the next question is procedural:

How much will the project affect the people inside the building?

What Should Property Owners Prepare Before a Commercial Roof Coating Project?

Even though this process is less invasive than a replacement, preparation is still essential to prevent tenant complaints and scheduling conflicts.

Tenant Communication Reduces Complaints and Scheduling Issues

Once eligibility is confirmed, communication becomes the next priority. Tenants should be informed about:

  • Project start and end dates
  • Potential temporary odors
  • Minor daytime noise
  • Access or parking adjustments

Clear communication early reduces complaints later.

Late Spring Through Early Fall Provides the Most Reliable Install Window

Timing matters. These systems require proper curing conditions. In Wichita, KS, late spring through early fall offers the most reliable installation window.

With preparation handled, the real concern becomes how tenants experience the project day-to-day.

How Disruptive Is a Roof Coating Compared to Replacement?

Now that we understand what the restoration process involves and how to prepare for it, let’s address tenant impact directly.

Most Roof Coating Projects Are Quiet Compared to Tear-Off Replacement

A roof coating is usually much quieter than a full roof replacement.

There is no large-scale removal of materials, nor are there large-scale machines moving materials. Most sound comes from:

  • Pressure washing or surface cleaning
  • Blowers used to dry and prepare the roof
  • Foot traffic
  • Equipment movement

Noise will be more concentrated around specific areas of the roof as the crew progresses. If the tenant has patient appointments, meetings, or other noise-sensitive groups, the contractor and property manager should plan around the most disruptive portions of the work before work begins.

A relatively quiet roofing project that tenants didn’t know about will still feel disruptive. Communication is essential when maintaining happy tenants.

See our tenant communication guide to learn more.

Odors Are Usually Temporary and Easier to Control Than Tenants Expect

Noise is only one part of the concern. Odor is often the bigger issue for office or medical tenants.

Some materials produce temporary smells during application that are not harmful. However, a smell that seems minor on the roof may feel more significant to a tenant inside a medical office, daycare, restaurant, salon, school, or office space. Below are a few factors that affect the coating’s odor:

  • Whether the product is water-based, solvent-based, or low-VOC
  • How close the work area is to HVAC units or air intake
  • Wind direction
  • Whether windows, doors, or vents are open or will regularly open

The contractor should identify all air intake and coordinate with the property manager how to protect tenants.

How Long Does a Commercial Roof Coating Take?

Duration is the next factor tenants care about.

A 20,000 to 40,000 square foot building may require:

  • 3 to 7 days
  • Additional time if repairs are needed

However, schedule depends on more than square footage. Access, requisite repairs, weather and crew size all influence the project’s timeline.

A rushed coating project may negatively affect the coating’s cure time and result in a failed project. Most contractors provide a project timeline that allows for a few days of weather-related incidentals — under-promise, overdeliver.

Phased installation ensures that disruption is controlled and predictable.

Do Tenants Need to Leave During a Coating Project?

Usually, no.

One of the advantages of coatings compared with many replacement projects is they do not require tenants to relocate or change their daily operations.

However, there are exceptions to this. A tenant may need to plan around the project if they operate:

  • A medical office
  • A daycare
  • A restaurant
  • A school
  • A business with scheduled client meetings or events

Even then, the solution is not usually for tenants to leave. It’s deliberate planning and communication, such as working outside of business hours or protecting air intake.

How Can Disruption Be Minimized?

Ultimately, disruption is less about the materials themselves and more about how the project is managed.

Experienced contractors reduce tenant impact by:

  • Working in controlled sections
  • Scheduling loud preparation early
  • Protecting HVAC intakes
  • Providing clear communication schedules

When properly planned, restoration work should not require tenant relocation or operational shutdown.

With disruption addressed, it is also important to understand which systems perform best in this region.

What Types of Commercial Roof Coatings Are Used in Wichita, KS?

Material selection influences not only durability but also installation experience.

Silicone Coatings Are Common in Kansas for UV and Ponding Water Resistance

Silicone systems resist ponding water and UV damage. They are common on flat roofs in Kansas due to rainfall cycles.

Acrylic Coatings Are Often Chosen for Reflectivity and Cooling Savings

Acrylic systems are highly reflective and reduce heat gain, making them attractive for energy savings.

Polyurethane Coatings Add Impact Resistance for Hail-Prone Areas

Polyurethane options provide added impact resistance, which can be beneficial in hail-prone areas.

Each system carries different curing characteristics and odor levels. That is why experienced commercial roof coating contractors evaluate both building use and tenant sensitivity before recommending a system.

Now let’s look at the broader pros and cons.

What Are the Pros and Cons of a Commercial Roof Coating?

Understanding the trade-offs helps property owners make informed decisions.

Pros

  • Lower cost than replacement
  • Minimal demolition
  • Faster project timelines
  • Improved energy efficiency
  • Cost-deferring

Cons

  • Not suitable for roofs with damaged substrate
  • Weather-sensitive installation
  • Requires proper surface preparation

When correctly applied, a coating can extend service life by 5 to 10 years depending on thickness and system type.

Even with these advantages, property owners still have practical questions. Let’s address those directly.

What Do Wichita, KS Property Owners Ask About Tenant Disruption?

Now that we’ve covered noise, odors, materials, and scheduling, here are the most common tenant-disruption questions commercial property owners ask before moving forward with restoration work.

How disruptive is this type of restoration project?

This type of restoration project is minimally disruptive compared to full replacement. Because there is no tear-off or large-scale demolition, most work remains confined to the roof surface with limited interior impact.

Will tenants notice strong odors during installation?

Tenants may notice temporary odors during application, but modern low-VOC materials significantly reduce indoor impact. Proper ventilation planning and scheduling outside peak hours further minimize disruption.

Can businesses stay open during installation?

Businesses can remain open during installation in most cases. Work is phased across sections of the building, allowing operations to continue without shutdown.

How long does the system typically last in Wichita, KS?

These systems typically last 10 to 20 years in Wichita, KS depending on thickness, material type, and ongoing maintenance. Regular inspections help maximize performance.

Does hail damage prevent restoration?

Hail damage does not automatically prevent restoration, but the existing membrane must remain structurally sound. Minor impact damage can often be repaired before application.

How do I know if my building qualifies?

Qualification requires a professional inspection to confirm the existing roof is dry and stable. If those conditions are met, restoration is often a cost-effective alternative to replacement.

Is a Commercial Roof Coating the Right Low-Disruption Solution?

A commercial roof coating does not have to mean tenant disruption. Compared to full replacement, restoration systems are quieter, faster, and less invasive.

With proper planning, clear communication, and experienced commercial roof coating contractors, most buildings remain fully operational during installation.

If you are evaluating options in Wichita, KS and want clear answers about noise, smells, and scheduling, Rhoden Roofing LLC brings certified expertise and tenant-focused project planning.

title.rendered: What Are Unvented Roofs (“Hot Roofs”) & When Are They Used?

content.rendered:
What is a Hot Roof System?
(Other Names include Unventilated Roof System, Closed Roof, and Spray Foam Roof Deck)

Most buildings with sloped roofs (as opposed to flat roofs) vent the underside of the roof deck to move heat and moisture up and out of the building. This is commonly paired with an open attic space, where the insulation for the building envelope sits on top of the ceiling of the top floor, and the rafter/truss space is empty above, all the way up to the roof deck. Intake ventilation at the soffits draws air in, while exhaust ventilation near the top (most common are box or ridge vents) lets air move up and out.

See a full case study on hot roofs
However, ventilation of the roof deck is not always possible, and may not be preferred. An unvented system applies insulation directly on the roof deck. Critically, they MUST be completely air impermeable, such as using closed-cell spray foam insulation, to a thickness where the inside surface will not be able to drop below the dew point and cause condensation even on the coldest day of the year. Insulation R-value requirements depend on climate zone: see below. Unvented roof systems are called “hot roofs” because they combine the roof system and insulation barrier into a single unit rather than two independent layers with moving air or an attic in between.

A full list of situations where a hot roof design may make sense is in the section below, but the applications largely boil down to two general categories: addressing limited space, and/or maximizing insulation value.

Note: for a complete list of the types of roof ventilation systems and how to identify them, see our article: What Type of Attic/Roof Ventilation System Do I Have? Note that many buildings have multiple ventilation system types; e.g. main house, a sun room or addition, detached garage, etc.

 

When Are Unvented and Hot Roof Systems Used?

A ‘hot roof’ design may be the best, or only viable solution in a variety of different situations. Broadly speaking, the use cases typically address either limited space constraints, the goal of maximizing insulation value, or both.

We have organized the list of unvented roof system applications from most common to least common. Especially in uncommon or niche scenarios, having this tool is essential to keep the building envelope safe/mold-free, and a relief to discover when so little information is available online or otherwise.

First, an aside about our use of the term “attic” within this article. In the field of building science, “attic” refers specifically to the unconditioned air cavity between the conditioned space and the roof deck. A true attic is a functioning part of the building system. If the top floor of a building has been converted to a conditioned living, storage, or mechanical space, it is no longer a true functioning attic, even if most people would continue to call it the “attic” in conversation (i.e., “attic bedroom”). In that example, the space behind the knee walls may still be a functioning attic, but it depends on insulation location and ventilation types.

  • Vaulted/cathedral ceilings with trapped rafter bays or non-continuous bays. For example:
    • Hip roofs where individual rafter bay do not connect to the upper ridge line for exhaust venting
    • Sunroom roof that meets a headwall of 2nd story above
    • Cathedral ceilings where individual rafter bays are interrupted by skylights
  • Vaulted/cathedral ceilings in historic homes with shallow rafter bays: especially those built with 2×4 or 2×6 construction which are too small to accommodate both ventilation chutes, which are typically 2” thick, and insulation within the rafter bay.
  • Small, unconnected roofs where traditional ventilation is unfeasible – e.g., bay window, dormers, bump-outs, cornice roofs.
  • Homeowners attempting to maximize insulation R-value — especially with vaulted ceilings, largely because the closed-cell spray foam used to insulate has the highest R-value per inch.
  • Roof areas over converted spaces, such as enclosing a former porch into conditioned space where the existing roof structure was not built with ventilation.
  • Converting historic wood shake to modern roofing if adding intake/exhaust is not viable. Wood roofs are built on slatted decking and “breathe” throughout, whereas modern roofs use a solid, continuous roof deck and require either ventilation or a hot roof design.
  • The lower section of multi-pitch roofs with limited access below – e.g. shallower first-floor roof that meets steeper 2nd-floor roofline.
  • Roofs ending in a headwall at the top where exhaust vents are deemed unsightly. Most common examples:
    • Headwall roofs on the street-facing side of a home
    • Original rooflines on front of a house where back of house has had a 2nd-floor “pop up” addition
  • Homes with multiple ridge/exhaust vent heights with a single, continuous attic space.
  • Shed roofs (the architectural shape, as in single-slope, not storage sheds), especially with cathedral ceilings or steeper roof pitches where exhaust venting at the top is limited by lack of shared ridge/attic, and eave vents are impractical from exposure to precipitation in the wind.
  • Buildings where intake venting is impractical or unwanted. Some examples include:
    • Mid-century modern ranch and atomic ranch style homes from the 1950s & 60s with no eaves and on-roof intake vents are not wanted
    • Homes with rafter-tail eaves rather than enclosed soffits and pocket vents or on-roof intake vents are deemed unsightly
    • Buildings with highly decorative eaves, including certain Victorian, Italianate, Gothic, or traditional Chinese and Japanese architecture
    • Geodesic dome or other uncommonly shaped rooflines, such as arched, catenary, or flared rooflines, butterfly roofs, or A-frame buildings.

Below are additional details on common scenarios cited above.

Vaulted Ceilings, or “Cathedral Ceilings”

Vaulted ceilings, also called cathedral ceilings, can either be vented or unvented; see our article What Type of Roof/Attic Ventilation System Do I Have.

Any vaulted ceiling with air-permeable insulation – such as fiberglass batts, net-and-blow insulation, open-cell foam, etc. – must have ventilation chutes or baffles against the roof deck to allow for adequate air flow. Those ventilation chutes must also be connected at the top and bottom to a functioning attic cavity or directly to exterior ventilation.

  • At the bottom (intake), a connected attic space in the eave, or behind a knee wall usually meet this requirement.
  • At the top (exhaust), each rafter bay can connect to a shared functioning attic space, such as a small triangular cavity at the ridge above a flat section of ceiling.
  • Alternatively, each bay can connect directly to exhaust venting, such as continuous ridge venting, to allow airflow.

If any of the conditions for a vented cathedral ceiling cannot be met, then the solution may be to seal the space with air-impermeable insulation and use an unvented, hot roof design.

 

Unvented Roof: Case Study

Figure 1: Rafters on this 1922 historic home are 2×4 construction, leaving little room for insulation without furring down the ceiling height. Additionally, roof hips and dormers close off rafter bays so that venting chutes would not be continuous from eave to ridge. Spaced plank decking is visible from the original wood shake roof, and much of the debris is still visible from when the wood roof was replaced with asphalt composite.

Figure 2: Eaves and rafter area cleaned out and prepared for closed-cell spray foam to enclose the air cavity and insulate. Spray foam functionally seals off any access to the rafter bay area, so electrical and any other chase items need to be run ahead of time before insulation.

Figure 3: Joist bays over the eaves need to be insulated past the exterior wall below to the same spec as the roof, in order to enclose the insulation envelope of the building.

Figure 4: Spray foam in place against the deck and ready for drywall/finishing.

Figure 5: At a minimum, spray foam’s R-value must be high enough to prevent the area from reaching dew point to prevent mold from growing: wet and stagnant usually produces mold. However, more insulation can always be added. Behind the knee walls, for example, air-permeable insulation was added to supplement the R-value of the spray foam. Finally, bathroom vents from below were routed to the exterior of the building to export any humidity. Venting above the roofline would be preferred, but in this case the shallow roof pitch allowed venting through the soffit.

Drywall can’t fasten into rafters obstructed by insulation, so the spray foam was applied shallower in the finished area for ease of drywall work. In the unfinished eave area behind the knee wall, extra insulation can be applied.

Note that heat will build up in the enclosed attic space in the eave (behind the knee wall). Maximizing insulation in that area can prevent heat transfer through the ceiling below, and insulating the back of the knee walls themselves can transfer heat into the finished room.

Figure 6: The small cavity between closed-cell foam and the back of the drywall can be filled with additional insulation (e.g., fiberglass, for sound attenuation and a little extra R-value). Closed-cell spray foam is rigid, so impact sounds (e.g., rain or tapping on the surface of a table) transfer clearly through it. Softer insulation is better at absorbing impact sounds. Roof systems are reasonably effective at attenuating ambient sounds (i.e., indirect sounds, like cars driving by), but not as effective at blocking impact sounds.

This is especially true for smooth, rigid roof materials like metal or composite tile.

How Are Unvented Roof Systems Built & Insulated?

Hot roofs have become more common in the last 20 years as closed-cell spray foam technology has improved and prices have become more affordable. The critical requirement for an unventilated hot roof system is getting air-impermeable insulation with an R-value that is sufficient to prevent the formation of any condensation on the bottom of the decking/insulation system, even on the coldest day of the year. In climate zone 4 (Southern Kansas and Missouri), this means a minimum of R-15. In climate zone 5 (Northern Kansas and Nebraska), this means a minimum of R-20. A higher R value is safer in case of inconsistencies in insulation thickness, wide variance of indoor humidity (which affects dew point), or extreme weather.

What Type of Insulation Is Used for Unvented Roofs?

The most common way to build a hot roof is with closed-cell spray foam (~R-6/inch) because of its air impermeability. The air-impermeable insulation layer must meet the R-value to prevent the inside face on the conditioned side from ever reaching the dew point. In the example where R-15 is needed, and using a spray foam rated at R6/inch, at least 2.5” minimum depth must be applied to the underside of the roof deck. Note that thermal bridging from rafters, nails, pipe penetrations, etc., will reduce the functional R-value at those points, so it is recommended to overshoot the minimum. Spray foam is expensive. Additionally, filling any thicker than the rafter opening adds labor cost (and mess) to shave down rigid foam before ceiling installation. Therefore, some people choose to apply 3” of depth with spray foam and then fill the remaining cavity space with compressible fiberglass batts.

In colder climates, such as the mountains or Northern parts of the US, some people use insulation in the roof deck system itself, such as rigid polyiso foam sandwiched between two layers of OSB.

It is also possible to design a hot roof with air-permeable insulation such as fiberglass batts or open-cell spray foam (which are cheaper), but it absolutely must have an air barrier like plastic sheeting to prevent condensation against cold roof decking or insulation. This somewhat riskier plan is more common in agricultural buildings or warehouses, where the cost savings over a large area are higher, or humidity/mold risk is lower – e.g., if industrial circulation fans constantly cycle air through the space. In an enclosed space such as above a vaulted drywall ceiling, the insulation must be air-impermeable.

Pros of Unvented Roof Systems

Why don’t all buildings use hot roofs? Conceptually, un-vented roof systems are the simplest insulation design: a single outer shell like an impermeable blanket on top of the building.

The “pros” from the detailed use case scenarios above can be summarized into:

  • There’s not enough space/you can’t feasibly ventilate. Basically, unvented is your only option.
  • Higher R-value of air-impermeable insulation can allow for better insulation in limited spaces.

Cons of Unvented Roof Systems

The “cons” list is longer. Each of these can be addressed, but you need to know what you’re doing to avoid surprises. In the right situation, hot roofs are the perfect solution. But here’s the precautions list; what to know about unvented roof systems and why they’re so much less common than vented roof systems:

  • Risk of mold. Incorrect installation, trapping air pockets, or failure to achieve an air-impermeable barrier to beyond the dew point will lead to condensation, moisture, and mold growth.
  • Cost. Spray foam is the most expensive insulation product available.
  • Environmental concerns. While increased insulation is good for lowering heating/cooling demands, different spray foam manufacturers have widely different environmental impacts related to product sourcing, propellant, and off-gassing, which releases dangerous VOCs. This leads to some controversy about the use of insulation products on the market.
  • Delayed discovery of roof leaks. Any material that is air-impermeable is also water-impermeable. Water leaking in through the roof surface may pool or get trapped/fail to dry out, leading to wood rotted decking or framing. Simply delaying how long it takes to notice roof leaks sounds like a good thing – the insulation will keep the water out of your finished ceiling, but there’s plenty above that subject to damage in the meantime. People with unvented roofs should be more diligent about inspecting their roof periodically or seasonally. Wet insulation also isn’t an effective insulator, effectively reducing its R-value.
  • Minimal exterior noise reduction, especially with vaulted ceilings against the roof, or low ceilings closer to occupants. Spray foam is rigid and lightweight, which are the two things that transfer sound. Rain drops, falling leaves, and other impacts are particularly noticeable through rigid materials. Imagine tapping on a full can versus tapping on an empty can: which is louder? This is another reason some people choose to use spray foam to pass the dew point barrier, then fill the remaining cavity with cheaper, soft insulation such as fiberglass batts to add mass and absorb resonance.
  • Difficulty repairing/replacing roof. If any decking needs to be removed during a future roofing project because of wood deterioration or direct damage, the spray foam will come out with it. That section requires the interior ceiling to be opened, re-sprayed, and drywall patched/textured/painted. If, for example, your home is positioned under a large cottonwood tree that likes to drop a big branch through your roof every few years, just know that those repairs will get a lot more expensive.
  • Limited wiring/ceiling access. Anything enclosed in spray foam becomes completely encased. New wiring via fishing tape etc., is functionally impossible in a foam ceiling. Wiring or pipes can be chipped out if encased in spray foam, but only if that section of ceiling is removed. – e.g., wiring or pipes encased by spray foam can make future modifications a nightmare.
  • Require intentionality with divided air pockets: e.g. eave area behind knee wall must be brought entirely within the insulation envelope (full roof deck plus soffit) if the ceiling/roofline above the knee wall is sealed.

A special note: Do not double insulate. We get customers who want to add insulation to their home to increase energy efficiency, and want to insulate the roof deck in addition to the ceiling above the top floor. Don’t do this. The building envelope – the boundary line between conditioned and unconditioned space – must be a single line. Double insulating traps air (and moisture) in between and becomes a breeding ground for mold and bacteria. This is like the Tupperware left at the back of the fridge. Don’t trap air.

 



Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

How common are unvented roof systems in Kansas?

Unvented roofs are relatively common for small roof sections, like bay windows or cornices. ~20% of homes have a small section of unvented roof. For larger areas, such as a whole slope, we only encounter it in about 5% of homes: usually newer custom builds or older (pre-1950) homes that have undergone major remodeling.

Is the roof built any different if the deck is insulated?

Other than the lack of ventilation components, no, the roof is installed the same way in an invented system.

Can you make just one section of a roof un-vented?

Yes – This is done sometimes with dormers that do not connect to primary ridges, or with individual rafter bays that are interrupted from bottom-to-top and block airflow, e.g. a skylight in a roof with a vaulted ceiling.
